title: Notes to Myself: A Week with Marcus Aurelius

source.author: Marcus Aurelius
source.rights: Long's 1862 translation is believed to be public domain in the United States. Standard Ebooks dedicates its own edition work to the public domain under CC0.
source.note: Checked against the Standard Ebooks source text on 2026-11-18. That edition does not print section numbers, so each section below is the standard book.section reference, mapped by paragraph order. Each lesson file holds its passage verbatim from that edition, with endnote markers and invisible word-joiner characters removed.

through_line: Week 1 asked what is actually yours. Week 2 asks how to keep that steady among other people. Nearly every passage this week is about them: the people who formed you, the ones who will irritate you, the ones who get in your way, the ones who wrong you, and how little their praise weighs. The running correction is that Stoicism is not a solitary or cold philosophy. Day 7 adds no new concept.
voice: Marcus writes to himself in the second person (Begin the morning by saying to thyself). This week every journal prompt asks the learner to do the same and address the entry to you.
end_of_week_artifact: Week 1 ended with a handbook of rules. Week 2 ends with the learner's own Book One. Marcus opens the Meditations with a list of what he learned from whom; the learner starts that list on Day 8 and finishes it on Day 14, alongside six entries written to themselves. The two weeks become the first two chapters of their journal.
end_message: That is Week 2. Your Book One and your notes to yourself are the second chapter of your journal.
handbook_title: Book One, and notes to myself

context_claims.note: Biographical lines the scripts will probably want. Listed here so the generator can reuse them word for word; each still needs your sign-off once.

items.claim: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 CE.
He wrote the Meditations in Greek, as notes to himself, and did not write them for publication.
Parts of it were probably written while he was on military campaign on the Danube frontier.
items.note: Book 1 ends with Among the Quadi at the Granua and Book 2 with This in Carnuntum. Those place notes are in the text; the campaign reading is not.

lessons.section: 1.1-1.3, and the closing line of Book 1
lessons.title: A List of Debts
lessons.concept: Character is learned from particular people, and Marcus opens his notebook by naming them
lessons.objective: Name three people and the specific thing each one taught you.
lessons.misconception_targeted: self-made: believing your character is something you built alone
lessons.practice: Notice one person today doing something you would like to learn. Write it the way Marcus would: From ___, ___.

lessons.title: The Morning Briefing
lessons.concept: Expect difficult people, put their faults down to ignorance, and remember you are made to work with them
lessons.objective: Prepare for a difficult person in a way that protects both your composure and your goodwill.
lessons.misconception_targeted: contempt: treating 'expect difficult people' as permission to look down on them
lessons.review_watch: The passage says people share the same portion of the divinity. Present that as Marcus's belief, not the narrator's.
lessons.practice: Before your next shared task, name the person most likely to irritate you and one way the two of you have to work together.

lessons.title: The Retreat You Carry
lessons.concept: You can withdraw into your own mind at any moment, if you keep a few brief principles ready to return to
lessons.objective: Write two brief principles you can return to in under a minute.
lessons.misconception_targeted: escapism: reading the inner retreat as a way of withdrawing from people or duties
lessons.focus: The section is long. Build the script on its opening (retire into yourself; keep your principles brief) and its closing paragraph (the two principles: things do not touch the soul, and everything changes). Leave the middle objections for a later week. The passage says the retreat sends you back to things, which is the answer to the escapism misreading.
lessons.practice: Once today, take a one-minute retreat: recall your two principles, then go back to what you were doing.

lessons.title: The Obstacle on the Road
lessons.concept: People can block what you do but not how you are disposed to act; the mind turns a hindrance into material for acting
lessons.objective: Find the action that a current obstacle still leaves open to you.
lessons.misconception_targeted: silver-lining: insisting the obstacle itself is good, rather than what you do with it
lessons.review_watch: Indifferent is a Stoic technical term here: neither good nor bad in itself. The script must not let it read as I don't care about people, which would undo the week's through-line. The passage opens with doing good to people and enduring them; keep that in.
lessons.practice: When someone gets in the way of a plan today, ask: what action is still open to me here?

lessons.title: The Best Revenge
lessons.concept: When someone wrongs you, the response that is yours is to not become like them
lessons.objective: Respond to a wrong without retaliating and without giving in.
lessons.misconception_targeted: doormat: thinking that refusing revenge means accepting mistreatment
lessons.format_notes: Same structure as the Week 1 bathhouse scenario: three moments, three choices each, paths fold back. Suggested setting: a colleague presents your idea as their own in a meeting. Moments: in the meeting, the message you write afterwards, and the next time you have to work with them. Tag retaliating choices mirroring and giving-in choices doormat. The untagged choice at each moment names the problem plainly without copying the behaviour. The retrieval question returns to Day 9: what reason did Marcus give for why people behave badly?
lessons.practice: If someone is rude to you today, ask before you reply: would this reply make me more like them?

lessons.title: The View from Above
lessons.concept: Changing the scale you look from shows how much of a worry is about reputation
lessons.objective: Separate the part of a worry that is about how you are seen from the part that is yours to act on.
lessons.misconception_targeted: nihilism: concluding that if everything looks small, nothing matters
lessons.format_notes: A rating before and after, five guided steps, then a multiple-choice check.
lessons.review_watch: The passage ends with nor reputation, nor anything else. Read alone, that sounds like nothing matters. The lesson reads it in context, where every item is about fame and being remembered.
lessons.practice: The next time praise or criticism stings today, take the view from above for ten seconds before you respond.

lessons.title: Be One
lessons.concept: Synthesis: stop describing the good person and be one
lessons.objective: Finish your Book One list and write one note to yourself that names an action rather than an ideal.
lessons.misconception_targeted: theory-as-practice: treating knowing about Stoicism as being a Stoic
lessons.format_notes: The passage is one sentence, so most of the script recaps the week. A recap claim may cite an earlier lesson's passage: give the claim a from field with that lesson's id, and check its support_span against that lesson's passage instead.
lessons.practice: Read back this week's six entries. Add one more line to your Book One list, then write a final note to yourself that begins with a verb.
